title: How the Composable Shelf Reinvents Marketing
gist: BCG proposes a 'Composable Shelf', a virtual reference layer above existing martech that records what each action, offer, and content asset is for, so AI agents can assemble individualized marketing interactions; BCG reports 3x ROI and 10x speed in client work. It argues consolidation alone cannot keep pace with AI-generated content and raises vendor lock-in, and lays out five organizational moves for governing agents.

insights.claim: BCG argues traditional campaign-based marketing is obsolete because applying AI to individual steps (content, audience, offer) leaves the fragmented, manually stitched workflow intact.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Point-solution AI marketing tools may deliver limited gains versus workflow-level redesign.
insights.quote: Traditional marketing had a good run, but it has long passed its expiration date.
insights.locator: Traditional marketing had a good run

insights.claim: BCG proposes a 'Composable Shelf': a virtual reference layer above existing asset, content, and offer systems that lets AI agents select and assemble approved actions, offers, and content for each customer.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Signals demand shifting toward metadata/orchestration layers rather than new monolithic marketing suites.
insights.quote: The marketing assets remain where they are; what the shelf adds is a record of what each piece is for and what it can be combined with based on what rules.
insights.locator: The Composable Shelf eliminates the shortcomings

insights.claim: Across BCG clients in retail, travel, banking, and healthcare services, the Composable Shelf approach has consistently delivered three times the ROI and ten times the speed from campaign initiation to implementation.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Claimed 3x ROI / 10x speed (consultant-reported, client work) suggests material marketing-efficiency upside for adopters.
insights.quote: BCG has consistently seen three times the ROI and ten times the speed from when the marketing campaign was initiated to implementation.
insights.locator: Many companies have tried to solve

insights.claim: In a bank autopay example, the shelf links the action (activating autopay) to a 1,000-point offer and approved emails and images, letting an agent assemble a customer-tailored interaction instead of choosing from pre-designed campaigns for broad groups.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Illustrates how agentic marketing shifts from segment campaigns to individualized interactions in financial services.
insights.locator: These links also enable agentic composition

insights.claim: Under the shelf model, marketers shift from assembling campaigns to curating the shelf, while the agent takes over assembly and deployment; the campaign is no longer the organizing principle of marketing work.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Implies restructuring of marketing labor and agency/services work toward curation and governance.
insights.quote: The campaign is no longer the organizing principle of their work; the shelf is.
insights.locator: The change in the marketers

themes.theme: Purpose metadata and the action library

insights.claim: Most marketing systems record what an asset is (format, rights, expiration date) but not what customer behavior it is meant to encourage; the shelf adds these missing purpose relationships.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The gap is purpose metadata, a wedge for vendors that tag intent rather than store more content.
insights.quote: Today’s marketing systems generally record what something is (e.g., a product image) but not what it is for.
insights.locator: Today’s marketing systems generally record

insights.claim: The shelf has three components: actions (what the business wants the customer to do), content (language and visuals), and offers (incentives such as discounts); every action needs content but not necessarily an offer.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A simple taxonomy for evaluating agentic-marketing platforms and data readiness.
insights.quote: Every action needs content, but it may or may not need an offer, and different content can be used with the same offer.
insights.locator: These connections are what turn

insights.claim: Automated pipelines pull references and existing tags from source systems, AI reconciles competing taxonomies into a common model and enriches metadata, and AI proposes action-offer-content relationships that marketers confirm.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Shows where AI adds value in data plumbing: taxonomy reconciliation and metadata enrichment.
insights.quote: AI reconciles competing taxonomies into a common model and enriches incomplete metadata.
insights.locator: Stocking the shelf does not mean

insights.claim: The action library is the one genuinely new asset the shelf requires, because desired customer actions today live in briefs, planning decks, and spreadsheets; BCG says it needs a senior marketing owner and should be treated as a marketing asset, not an IT one.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Ownership of the action library becomes a strategic control point inside marketing organizations.
insights.quote: Treat it as a marketing asset, not an IT one.
insights.locator: Give the action library an owner

themes.theme: Why consolidation and platform lock-in fall short

insights.claim: BCG says marketing-technology consolidation, the decade-long response to fragmentation, yields only incremental task improvements and suffers three flaws: it can never be finished, never be comprehensive, and can't keep pace with AI-generated content volume.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Challenges the thesis behind single-suite marketing cloud consolidation strategies.
insights.quote: Because AI continuously generates content, the volume of material grows too fast to be effectively migrated and organized.
insights.locator: A closer look reveals three shortcomings

insights.claim: Consolidation was designed to help people manage and retrieve assets, not to give an agent the purpose and relationships it needs; moving a file into a common repository does not record the customer action it is meant to drive.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Existing DAM/repository investments may not translate into agentic readiness.
insights.quote: Even with agentic AI, consolidation tells marketers what information they have, not what it is for.
insights.locator: Agentic AI introduces yet another challenge

insights.claim: Concentrating marketing operations in a single platform raises vendor lock-in risk, binding the company to that vendor's roadmap, metadata model, and release schedule.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A headwind narrative for all-in-one marketing platform vendors and a tailwind for interoperable layers.
insights.quote: the more the company must work within that vendor's roadmap, metadata model, and release schedule.
insights.locator: Consolidation can also increase the risk

insights.claim: Because the shelf is a common catalog not tied to one platform, companies can swap content, offer, decision, or activation systems without losing accumulated taxonomy and purpose records; BCG calls it the inverse of vendor lock-in.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Value accrues to the reference layer, potentially lowering switching costs and pricing power of underlying platforms.
insights.quote: the Composable Shelf is the inverse of vendor lock-in
insights.locator: This makes the Composable Shelf

insights.claim: BCG frames consolidation and the shelf as self-reinforcing rather than competing: consolidation simplifies existing systems while the shelf adds the layer needed for agentic activation, and the shelf need not wait for consolidation to finish.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Adoption can proceed alongside ongoing martech programs, easing enterprise rollout.
insights.quote: A Composable Shelf starts by moving nothing.
insights.locator: So far, every fix using consolidation

insights.claim: The shelf holds ingredients at three levels tagged the same way: individual building blocks (offers, headlines, images), complete touchpoints (an approved email), and designed sequences (launch, onboarding, loyalty milestone), so not every interaction must be decomposed.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Lowers disruption to content teams, who keep their tools, processes, and approval chains.
insights.locator: Composability also does not mean

themes.theme: Governing agents: rollout playbook for leaders

insights.claim: BCG says building the shelf's technology is the easier part; the harder work is organizational: agreeing on desired customer actions, writing rules upfront, and ceding decisions to agents.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Adoption bottlenecks are organizational, favoring consulting and change-management spend over pure software.
insights.quote: Building the technology behind the Composable Shelf is the easier part
insights.locator: What Using the Composable Shelf Means

insights.claim: BCG recommends starting with a test on one customer behavior, measuring how long it takes and how many people are needed to find all relevant offers, content, and constraints, then turning that test into the first shelf pilot.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Provides a low-cost diagnostic for gauging an organization's agentic-marketing readiness.
insights.quote: an agent can only work with what it can find and understand.
insights.locator: Run the test, then make it the pilot

insights.claim: Legal and brand teams should write rules upfront on region, rights, embargoes, and eligibility, so the agent applies them each time it assembles an interaction instead of routing every finished interaction through approval.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Shifting compliance to rule-setting removes a key throughput bottleneck in personalized marketing.
insights.quote: Bring legal and brand teams in to write the rules, not review the output.
insights.locator: Bring legal and brand teams in

insights.claim: Agent autonomy should widen gradually: let agents compose freely only from preapproved ingredients for always-on, lower-stakes actions, keep designed sequences intact, retain human approval where regulation or brand exposure requires, and expand latitude as results come in.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect staged, slow autonomy expansion, especially in regulated sectors like banking and healthcare.
insights.quote: Expand the agent’s latitude as the results come in, not before.
insights.locator: Decide what the agent may do on its own

insights.claim: BCG argues marketing performance metrics must shift from campaign counts and campaign performance toward whether the shelf covers priority customer actions with current approved content and offers, and how those ingredients perform when agents use them.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Changing KPIs signal a reorganization of marketing roles and budget allocation.
insights.locator: Change the job, then change how success

insights.claim: BCG advises starting with the shelf rather than the intelligence engine, since engines and vendors may be replaced while the shelf's options, relationships, and rules persist; none of the five moves requires choosing a new platform first.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Suggests durable value sits in proprietary marketing data structures, not in any given AI engine vendor.
insights.quote: That is why the place to start is the shelf rather than the engine.
